01.note: Moths got into Rabbi Hiyya's flax, and he came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi for advice. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him to slaughter a bird over the tub of water where the flax was soaking: the moths would smell the blood and leave. The Gemara asks how this was allowed, since a baraita says that one who slaughters because he needs the blood must still cover it. Two traditions answer: Rav Dimi reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him first to make the bird a tereifa and then slaughter it, and Ravin reported that he told him to tear loose its windpipe and gullet instead of slaughtering it.
01.why: The mishna says one who stabs an animal or tears loose its windpipe and gullet need not cover the blood; this case shows that rule put to practical use, and the Gemara goes on to ask why Rav Dimi's version did not simply say to tear the organs loose.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage whose flax was infested with moths; he asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi what to do.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he advised using a bird's blood to drive the moths away.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from Eretz Yisrael and reported one version of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's instruction.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: A Sage who came from Eretz Yisrael and reported a second version of the instruction.

terms.meaning: A Torah commandment: when a wild animal or bird is slaughtered, its blood must be covered with earth rather than left exposed or used.
An animal or bird with a fatal injury or defect; it is forbidden to eat even if properly slaughtered, and slaughtering it does not require covering the blood.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

02.note: Rabbi Abba, son of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, and Rabbi Zeira were standing in the marketplace of Caesarea at the door of the study hall. Rabbi Ami came out, found them, and scolded them: had he not told them not to stand outside while the study hall was in session, in case someone inside needed help with a point of law? Rabbi Zeira went in; Rabbi Abba did not. Inside, the students were puzzling over which of two rulings by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was the later one, and Rabbi Zeira complained that they had not told him while he was outside, so he could have asked the elder, Rabbi Abba, who might have heard the answer from his father, who reviewed his learning before Rabbi Yohanan every thirty days.
02.why: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled once like Rabbi Meir and once like the Rabbis on slaughtering the offspring of an animal slaughtered by a deaf-mute, imbecile or minor; the Gemara asks which ruling came later, and this incident shows the question was asked but left open.

people.name: Rabbi Abba, son of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Called the elder here; he stayed outside the study hall and might have known the answer from his father.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Stood outside with Rabbi Abba, then went into the study hall when scolded.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Came out of the study hall and rebuked the two for standing outside during study.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Rabbi Abba's father, who reviewed his studies before Rabbi Yohanan every thirty days.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The teacher before whom Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba reviewed his learning.

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages and students gathered to learn and debate Jewish law.
Jewish law; here, a specific legal ruling someone might need explained.

03.note: Rav Beruna and Rav Hananel, students of Rav, were sitting at a meal while Rav Yeiva the Elder stood over them serving. They asked him for a cup of wine over which to recite Grace after Meals, then changed their minds and asked for a cup to drink. Rav Yeiva the Elder told them that Rav had said: once a person says 'Give me a cup to say the blessing,' he is forbidden to drink more wine, because he has declared his meal over.
03.why: Rabbi Hanina says even Rabbi Yehuda, who requires covering a wild animal's blood before slaughtering a bird, allows one blessing for both. This incident is raised to argue the pause needs a new blessing; the Gemara rejects it, since one can slaughter with one hand and cover with the other.

people.name: Rav Beruna
people.about: A student of Rav, dining with Rav Hananel.

people.name: Rav Hananel
people.about: A student of Rav, dining with Rav Beruna.

people.name: Rav Yeiva the Elder
people.about: Served the two students at their meal and told them Rav's rule about the cup of blessing.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher of the two students, whose ruling Rav Yeiva quotes.

terms.meaning: The blessings said at the end of a meal with bread, often recited over a cup of wine.

04.note: A heretic told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that the verse 'He Who forms the mountains and He Who creates the wind' shows two separate gods. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called him an imbecile and pointed to the verse's end: 'The Lord, the God of hosts, is His name.' The heretic asked for three days to find a rebuttal, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fasted those three days. As he sat down to eat, he was told a heretic was at the door. It was another heretic, who said the first had found no answer, thrown himself from the roof and died. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi invited him to dine, then offered him the cup of blessing or forty gold coins. He chose the cup, and a Divine Voice declared the cup of blessing worth forty gold coins. Rabbi Yitzhak says the man's family, bar Luyyanus, is still prominent in Rome.
04.why: Rabban Gamliel fined a man ten gold coins for taking another's mitzva of covering blood, and the Gemara asks whether the fine pays for the mitzva or for its blessing. The Divine Voice's forty coins for a four-blessing Grace after Meals suggests ten coins per blessing.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he answered the heretic's argument from the verse and fasted while awaiting his rebuttal.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who reports that the second heretic's family still exists among the prominent families of Rome.

terms.meaning: Here, someone who argued against the Jewish belief in one God, using verses of the Bible to claim there were several gods.
The cup of wine over which Grace after Meals is recited; the one who leads the blessing holds it and drinks from it.
A voice from Heaven that, in rabbinic stories, announces God's view of an event.

05.note: Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya was peeling the membranes off a spleen for Levi, son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya, cutting them only from the upper surface. Levi told him to go down further. Levi's father, Rav Huna bar Hiyya, came in, found him saying this, and told him that his own mother's father, Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, had said in the name of Rav that the Torah forbids only the membranes on the thick, upper surface of the spleen.
05.why: The Gemara has just listed the membranes forbidden for eating, including the spleen's because it contains forbidden fat; this incident asks how much of that membrane is forbidden, and Levi goes on to challenge his father with a baraita.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya
people.about: Was preparing a spleen for Levi by peeling off its membranes.

people.name: Levi
people.about: Son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya; he told Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya to cut deeper.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: Levi's father, who corrected him by quoting Levi's maternal grandfather.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Levi's mother's father, who transmitted a ruling in the name of Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage in whose name the ruling about the spleen's membranes was given.

terms.meaning: Thin layers of tissue on the spleen that the Sages considered forbidden fat, so they had to be removed before the meat could be eaten.

06.note: Shmuel was crossing a river on a ferry. He told his attendant to give the ferryman a suitable gift as payment. The attendant did so, and Shmuel became angry with him. The story itself does not say why.
06.why: The Gemara is explaining why a Jew may not send a gentile a cut-up thigh with its sciatic nerve still in it: it would deceive him, and Shmuel forbade deceiving even a gentile. That ruling, the Gemara says, was inferred from this incident, and it then debates what Shmuel was angry about.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who was crossing a river by ferry and became angry at how his attendant paid the ferryman.

terms.meaning: A Sage's personal servant or student who carried out errands for him.

07.note: A man sent a friend a barrel of wine with a layer of oil floating on top, so it looked like a barrel of oil. The friend, thinking he had oil, invited guests to share it. When they arrived and he found the barrel was wine, he hanged himself in his shame.
07.why: A baraita is listing ways one may not mislead others, such as passing off a dead animal's hide as a slaughtered one's; it rules that one may not send wine with oil floating on top, and this incident shows the harm such a deception can do.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

08.note: In years of famine a man invited three guests but had only three eggs to set before them. His son came in, and each guest in turn gave the boy his portion. The father came and found the boy with one egg in his mouth and two in his hand, and struck him to the ground, and the boy died. When the mother saw, she went up to the roof, fell and died, and the father too went up to the roof, fell and died. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov said that three Jewish souls were killed over this matter.
08.why: A baraita rules that guests may not give their host's son or daughter food from their plates without the host's permission; this incident is its warning. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's comment shows the whole baraita is his.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who said three Jewish souls were killed over guests giving food to a host's child.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

09.note: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Nahman, was traveling from Sikhra to Bei Mehoza when he met Rava and Rav Safra heading toward Sikhra. Thinking they had come out to greet him, he asked why the Rabbis had troubled themselves to come so far. Rav Safra told him they had not known he was coming, and would have gone to more trouble if they had. Afterward Rava asked Rav Safra why he had said this and upset Mar Zutra. Rav Safra answered that otherwise they would have misled him, and Rava replied that Mar Zutra had misled himself.
09.why: Butchers announced a tereifa for gentiles only as 'meat for the soldiers'; the Gemara answers the charge that this deceives them by saying they deceive themselves, and this incident proves that letting someone mislead himself is permitted.

people.name: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Nahman
people.about: Was traveling to Bei Mehoza and assumed the two Sages had come out to greet him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Was traveling with Rav Safra; he faulted Rav Safra for upsetting Mar Zutra.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Told Mar Zutra frankly that they had not come out to greet him.

10.note: A Jewish butcher told another man that if he had made peace with him, he would have given him a cut from the fattened bull he prepared the day before. The man replied that he had eaten the finest of it anyway, since a certain gentile had bought some and fed it to him. The butcher said he had prepared two bulls, and the one the man ate was a tereifa. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked whether, because of this imbecile who acted improperly, they should forbid all the meat in the butcher shops. Others report that he said the butcher only meant to cause his fellow distress.
10.why: The Gemara has been discussing selling non-kosher meat to gentiles. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's reaction fits his ruling that meat found with a gentile is permitted where the butchers are Jewish, and the Gemara goes on to ask why, in the second version, his ruling rests on the butcher's spite.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he refused to forbid all the butcher shops because of this one butcher.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect; its meat is not kosher even if it was properly slaughtered.
An ox specially fed to be fat, prized for its meat.

11.note: Rav was sitting at the ford of the Ishtetit River when he saw a man cleaning an animal's head in the water. The head fell from his hands, so he brought a basket, cast it into the river and pulled out two heads. Rav asked whether it commonly happens that one loses one thing and finds two, and forbade both heads to him. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi asked Rav whether forbidden meat is common and permitted meat not, and he answered that forbidden meat is more common.
11.why: The Gemara has been testing Rav's view that meat out of one's sight becomes forbidden; it explains that he never stated this outright, and the rule was inferred from this incident. It then asks whether the incident proves much, since that spot was a port of gentiles.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who watched the man fish two animal heads out of the river and forbade both.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Questioned Rav's ruling together with Rav Asi.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Questioned Rav's ruling together with Rav Kahana.

terms.meaning: A shallow place where a river can be crossed; here, a spot on the riverbank where people came to wash things.

12.note: Rav was traveling to the home of his son-in-law, Rav Hanan, and saw the ferry coming toward him just as he arrived; he said this meant a good day awaited him where he was going. At Rav Hanan's gate he looked through a crack in the door and saw an animal hanging, ready to be cooked. He knocked, and everyone came out to greet him, the butchers too, while Rav never took his eyes off the meat. He told them that if they had relied on their own watching just then, they would have fed forbidden meat to his daughter's sons. Even so, Rav did not eat from that meat.
12.why: The Gemara has asked how Rav ever ate meat, given his view that meat left out of sight becomes forbidden. Here he kept it in sight himself, so the Gemara asks why he still refused it: perhaps for treating the ferry as an omen, or because it was an optional feast.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage visiting his son-in-law; he kept watch over the meat but did not eat it.

people.name: Rav Hanan
people.about: Rav's son-in-law, at whose home the meal was being prepared.

terms.meaning: A boat carrying travelers across a river; Rav took its arrival just as he reached the bank as a good sign.

13.note: As long as Rav lived, Rabbi Yohanan in Eretz Yisrael addressed his letters 'To our Master who is in Babylonia.' After Rav died, he wrote to Shmuel as 'our colleague in Babylonia.' Shmuel, stung, sent him the calculation of leap years for the next sixty years, but Rabbi Yohanan said this only showed he knew arithmetic. Then Shmuel sent him rulings on doubtful cases of tereifot that filled thirteen camel loads, and Rabbi Yohanan said: I have a Master in Babylonia; I will go and see him. Before setting out he asked a child to recite his verse, and the child said, 'Now Samuel was dead.' Rabbi Yohanan concluded that Shmuel had died, and did not go.
13.why: The Gemara has just said that Rabbi Yohanan would seek a sign by asking a child for his verse; this is an example. The Gemara then adds that Shmuel had not died; the sign came so Rabbi Yohanan would be spared the hard journey.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage in Eretz Yisrael who wrote letters to the leading Sages of Babylonia.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage in Babylonia whom Rabbi Yohanan addressed as 'our Master' while he lived.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage in Babylonia who set out to prove to Rabbi Yohanan that he was his master.

terms.meaning: Years in which an extra month is added to the Jewish calendar so the lunar months stay in step with the seasons; working them out required expert calculation.
Plural of tereifa: animals with a fatal injury or defect, whose meat is not kosher; deciding doubtful cases takes great expertise.

14.note: A man called bar Peyoli was standing before Shmuel, removing the sciatic nerve from an animal's leg, cutting it out without scraping away the surrounding flesh. Shmuel told him to go down further, and said that if he had not been watching, bar Peyoli would have fed him forbidden meat. Bar Peyoli was so frightened that the knife fell from his hand. Shmuel told him not to be afraid: whoever taught him had taught him in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
14.why: The mishna records a dispute: the first view requires scraping away flesh to remove the whole sciatic nerve, while Rabbi Yehuda says cutting it out is enough. This incident opens the Gemara's discussion, with Shmuel following the first view, and Rav Sheshet then asks which part bar Peyoli had left.

people.name: bar Peyoli
people.about: A man removing the sciatic nerve from a leg of meat in front of Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who corrected bar Peyoli's work and then reassured him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage of the mishna whose more lenient method bar Peyoli had been taught.

terms.meaning: A nerve in an animal's hind leg that the Torah forbids eating, in memory of Jacob's injury when he wrestled the angel; it must be cut out before the meat is eaten.

15.note: In the home of the Exilarch, some animal thighs were salted with the sciatic nerve still inside. Ravina ruled the meat forbidden, and Rav Aha bar Rav Ashi ruled it permitted. They went and asked Mar bar Rav Ashi, who told them: My father permitted it.
15.why: Shmuel ruled that a thigh cooked with its sciatic nerve is entirely forbidden, but a roasted one may be eaten once the nerve is reached. The question is whether salting counts as cooking, and the Gemara goes on to show Ravina's strict ruling is hard to square with Shmuel.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who ruled the salted thighs forbidden.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who ruled the salted thighs permitted.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Was asked to decide, and reported that his father permitted such meat.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a hereditary leader recognized by the government.
A nerve in an animal's hind leg that the Torah forbids eating; it must be removed before the meat is eaten.

16.note: Half an olive-bulk of forbidden fat fell into a pot of kosher meat. Mar bar Rav Ashi thought it would be enough for the meat to be thirty half-olive-bulks, half the usual ratio. His father, Rav Ashi, said to him: Have I not told you not to treat measures lightly, even rabbinic ones? He added that Rabbi Yohanan said even a half-measure is forbidden by Torah law, so the fat is cancelled only by sixty times its volume of meat.
16.why: The Gemara is discussing how forbidden food that falls into a mixture is cancelled, generally by sixty times its volume; just before, Rav Ashi was challenged over measuring with what the pot had absorbed, and this second incident about the measure follows.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Son of Rav Ashi; he wanted to use a smaller measure to cancel the fat.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Mar bar Rav Ashi's father, who rebuked him for treating measures lightly.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage quoted by Rav Ashi: even half the forbidden amount is prohibited by Torah law.

terms.meaning: A standard measure of volume, about the size of an olive; it is the smallest amount of forbidden food for which one is punished.
Certain fats of cattle, sheep and goats that the Torah forbids eating.
Less than the minimum amount that brings punishment; Rabbi Yohanan holds that eating it is still forbidden by the Torah.

17.note: A man came before Rabbi Hanina with a question while Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina sat at the gate. When the man came out, Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina asked what Rabbi Hanina had said, and the man said he had permitted it. Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina told him to bring it before Rabbi Hanina again. Rabbi Hanina said: Who is this who is bothering me? Go tell the one sitting at the gate that sciatic nerves do not impart flavor.
17.why: The mishna measures whether a sciatic nerve cooked in a thigh flavors the meat, while a baraita cites the view that nerves impart no flavor at all; this incident shows Rabbi Hanina ruling by that view, which the Gemara adopts as the law.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who permitted the man's meat and sent word that sciatic nerves do not impart flavor.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina
people.about: Was sitting at the gate and sent the man back to Rabbi Hanina to ask again.

terms.meaning: A nerve in an animal's hind leg that the Torah forbids eating; it must be removed before the meat is eaten.
A forbidden food cooked with permitted food makes the mixture forbidden only if its taste passes into it; if nerves have no taste, the rest of the meat stays permitted.

18.note: Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Mesharshiyya, visited the house of Rav Ashi. They brought him cheese and he ate it, then brought him meat and he ate it without washing his hands in between. The household objected that Agra had taught only that bird meat and cheese may be eaten freely, which implies that meat of cattle and cheese may not. Rav Yitzhak answered that Agra's rule applies at night, but by day he can see that nothing is left on his hands.
18.why: The Gemara has just quoted Agra, father-in-law of Rabbi Abba, that bird meat and cheese may be eaten without washing hands or wiping the mouth between them; this incident limits that teaching.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Mesharshiyya
people.about: A visitor at Rav Ashi's house who ate meat after cheese without washing his hands.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage whose household served Rav Yitzhak and questioned what he did.

people.name: Agra
people.about: Father-in-law of Rabbi Abba, whose teaching about bird meat and cheese the household quoted.

terms.meaning: Jewish law forbids eating meat and dairy together, so the Sages discuss what must be done, such as washing hands, between eating one and the other.

19.note: Abaye would inspect his property every day. One day he met his sharecropper carrying a load of wood and asked where he was taking it. The sharecropper said: To the Master's house. Abaye, knowing the man meant to keep the wood for himself, told him: The Sages already got there before you.
19.why: Shmuel has just said that one who inspects his property every day will find a coin, meaning it will pay off; Abaye's encounter shows that advice at work.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who inspected his property every day and caught his sharecropper with the wood.

terms.meaning: A tenant who farms another person's land in exchange for a share of the crop.

20.note: Rav Asi inspected his property every day and asked where were all the coins that Mar Shmuel had promised. One day he saw a water channel that had burst and was flooding his land. He took off his cloak, rolled it up and stuffed it into the gap, then shouted, and people came and sealed the hole. He said: I have found all of Mar Shmuel's coins.
20.why: Shmuel has said that one who inspects his property every day will find an asteira coin; after Abaye's story, this is a second case showing that the daily check pays off.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: A Sage who inspected his property daily and doubted it was worth it, until he found the flood.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who taught that inspecting one's property every day will turn up a coin.

terms.meaning: A small coin; Shmuel's saying means that regular checks on one's property bring a reward.
